subtopics.title: Solve linear inequalities
subtopics.exposition: A linear inequality is similar to a linear equation in that the largest exponent of a variable is 1. The only difference between solving an inequality and solving an equation occurs when there is a multiplication or a division that involves a minus sign. Dividing both sides of 8>6 by -2 gives -4>-3, which is not true, so the inequality sign must be switched around, giving -4<-3. When we divide or multiply both sides of an inequality by a negative number, the direction of the inequality changes. For example, if x<1, then -x>-1. For an equation such as 2x+2=1 there is only a single value of x for which the equation is true. For an inequality there is a range of values for which the inequality is true; this is the main difference between an equation and an inequality. The methods used to solve linear inequalities are similar to those used to solve linear equations. To solve the inequality 2x+2<=1, rearrange to 2x<=1-2, simplify to 2x<=-1, and then x<=-1/2. To solve 6-r>2, rearrange and solve for -r: -r>2-6, giving -r>-4. From -r>-4, multiply and reverse the inequality sign, giving r<4. To solve 4q+3<2(q+3), first expand the bracket, giving 4q+3<2q+6. Rearrange and solve for q: 4q+3<2q+6 becomes 4q-2q<6-3, giving 2q<3. Divide both sides of 2q<3 by 2, giving q<3/2, with the inequality sign unchanged.

subtopics.title: Number line and interval notation
subtopics.exposition: The answer to an equation or an inequality can be represented on a number line. The answer x<=-1/2 is represented in interval notation as (-infinity;-1/2]. The solution r<4 is represented in interval notation as (-infinity;4). The solution q<3/2 is represented in interval notation as (-infinity;3/2). In interval notation an interval is written with its two endpoints separated by a semicolon inside brackets, for example (4, 12). Round brackets indicate that the number is not included. A square bracket indicates that the number is included. Round brackets are always used for positive and negative infinity. The interval (4, 12) includes all real numbers greater than but not equal to 4 and less than but not equal to 12. The interval (-infinity;-1) includes all real numbers less than, but not equal to, -1. The interval [1, 13) includes all real numbers greater than or equal to 1 and less than but not equal to 13.

subtopics.title: Solve compound inequalities
subtopics.exposition: To solve the compound inequality 5<=x+3<8, subtract 3 from all the parts of the inequality, giving 2<=x<5. The answer to a compound inequality such as 2<=x<5 is represented on a number line. The solution 2<=x<5 is represented in interval notation as [2, 5).

claims.claim: A linear inequality is similar to a linear equation in that the largest exponent of a variable is 1.
The methods used to solve linear inequalities are similar to those used to solve linear equations.
The only difference between solving an inequality and solving an equation occurs when there is a multiplication or a division that involves a minus sign.
Dividing both sides of 8>6 by -2 gives -4>-3, which is not true, so the inequality sign must be switched around, giving -4<-3.
When we divide or multiply both sides of an inequality by a negative number, the direction of the inequality changes.
For example, if x<1, then -x>-1.
We cannot divide or multiply an inequality by a variable.
To solve the inequality 2x+2<=1, rearrange to 2x<=1-2, simplify to 2x<=-1, and then x<=-1/2.
For an equation such as 2x+2=1 there is only a single value of x for which the equation is true.
For an inequality there is a range of values for which the inequality is true; this is the main difference between an equation and an inequality.
The answer to an equation or an inequality can be represented on a number line.
In interval notation an interval is written with its two endpoints separated by a semicolon inside brackets, for example (4, 12).
Round brackets indicate that the number is not included.
A square bracket indicates that the number is included.
Round brackets are always used for positive and negative infinity.
The interval (4, 12) includes all real numbers greater than but not equal to 4 and less than but not equal to 12.
The interval (-infinity;-1) includes all real numbers less than, but not equal to, -1.
The interval [1, 13) includes all real numbers greater than or equal to 1 and less than but not equal to 13.
Interval notation can only be used to represent an interval of real numbers.
The answer x<=-1/2 is represented in interval notation as (-infinity;-1/2].
To solve 6-r>2, rearrange and solve for -r: -r>2-6, giving -r>-4.
From -r>-4, multiply and reverse the inequality sign, giving r<4.
The solution r<4 is represented in interval notation as (-infinity;4).
To solve 4q+3<2(q+3), first expand the bracket, giving 4q+3<2q+6.
Rearrange and solve for q: 4q+3<2q+6 becomes 4q-2q<6-3, giving 2q<3.
Divide both sides of 2q<3 by 2, giving q<3/2, with the inequality sign unchanged.
The solution q<3/2 is represented in interval notation as (-infinity;3/2).
To solve the compound inequality 5<=x+3<8, subtract 3 from all the parts of the inequality, giving 2<=x<5.
The answer to a compound inequality such as 2<=x<5 is represented on a number line.
The solution 2<=x<5 is represented in interval notation as [2, 5).
